rationale: B wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its cleanest angle, “How big does a purchase have to be before Pay by Bank beats a card?”, turns Plaid’s 70% claim into a reportable math test, while A reaches for “FedNow just got its most significant commercial test” without proof that it is most significant. A has newsroom shape, but B has the adult virtue here: restraint.
gaps_in_A: “FedNow just got its most significant commercial test” is an unsupported superlative. The update says Pay by Bank uses FedNow rails; it does not prove significance, volume, or market rank.
“Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes. Now it wants to own the payment.” imports company history and strategic intent that are not in the supplied facts.
“competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen” is not grounded in the update. It may be plausible market context, but plausible is not evidence.

“verified connections to 12,000 financial institutions” muddies the fact pattern. The update says Plaid connects to over 12,000 institutions; it does not say those connections are all verified for this payment product.
gaps_in_B: “Plaid turns 12,000 bank connections into a payments network” is dismissed as a duplicate too quickly. A tightly grounded company-strategy angle could be distinct from the card-network conflict.
“bank-to-bank payments in front of shoppers” pushes toward checkout UX, but the update gives no detail on shopper experience, authentication flow, refunds, or friction.
“which public infrastructure wins” is a little grand. FedNow can be the protagonist, but the supplied facts support a commercial adoption data point, not a victory lap.
